		<title>Introducing Build-A-Chip-Bench: From Workload Specification to GDS</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/introducing-build-a-chip-bench-from-workload-specification-to-gds/</link>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Evaluate AI agents from workload specification through GDS layout, using open-source tools and an open-source PDK to assess their ability to complete the chip-design workflow. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/introducing-build-a-chip-bench-from-workload-specification-to-gds/">Introducing Build-A-Chip-Bench: From Workload Specification to GDS</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Existing chip design benchmarks test isolated steps, such as writing RTL from a specification, and are increasingly saturated. ChipAgents is developing Build-A-Chip-Bench with contributions from Nvidia to the benchmark suite and scoring rubric. The benchmark evaluates AI agents from workload specification through GDS layout, using open-source tools and an open-source PDK to assess their ability to complete the chip-design workflow. Each design must pass a hard gate, covering functional correctness against a hidden verification IP as well as routability, hold timing, and DRC, and designs that pass are scored on PPA against the task’s constraints. The best agent passes the hard gate on 65% of tasks and reaches an overall score of 16.6%. Frontier agents struggle to revisit earlier decisions, protect working behavior while optimizing, and plan around slow tool runs.</p>
<p>Read <a href="https://chipagents.ai/research/build-a-chip-bench">more here</a>.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/introducing-build-a-chip-bench-from-workload-specification-to-gds/">Introducing Build-A-Chip-Bench: From Workload Specification to GDS</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>Foundations of Power Management in the Age of AI</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/foundations-of-power-management-in-the-age-of-ai/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/foundations-of-power-management-in-the-age-of-ai/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Movellus]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 07:03:10 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[System-Level Design]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[AI data center]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[control loops]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Make every layer of your hardware PDN-aware and reach your maximum compute density.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/foundations-of-power-management-in-the-age-of-ai/">Foundations of Power Management in the Age of AI</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>In an AI datacenter, 50 mV of voltage margin can be worth about 270 racks of compute per gigawatt of input electricity. To show how, this paper models two facilities that run the same Vera Rubin NVL72 racks at the same clock speeds, one at 0.80 V and one at 0.75 V. On published Vera Rubin power figures, the second draws about 8% less power per GPU and about 17 kW less per rack.</p>
<p>Margin is the supply voltage added above what the silicon needs to cover the worst-case voltage droop. Evolving AI workloads make that margin larger and harder to predict. As a result, platform and silicon teams often over-margin to compensate, costing them compute density and token throughput, while teams that margin too little see failures in the field.</p>
<p>Power delivery network (PDN) design in the age of AI takes a systematic approach to power management. This paper distills the foundation of that approach into four axioms, drawn from work with customers in AI and high-performance computing (HPC).</p>
<p><strong>AXIOM 1</strong>: Test error must be minimized</p>
<p><strong>AXIOM 2</strong>: Power envelopes must factor in both evolving workloads and PDN dynamics</p>
<p><strong> AXIOM 3</strong>: AI systems require reactive or preemptive Ldi/dt (droop) mitigation</p>
<p><strong>AXIOM 4</strong>: Co-architected control loops are a necessity for systems</p>
<p>Movellus addresses the four axioms in one stack through its Aeonic platform. The platform helps teams set the foundation of proper power architecture in the age of AI.</p>
<p>Read <a href="https://www.movellus.com/col-req/?collateralVal=Whitepaper%20-%20Foundations%20of%20Power%20Management%20in%20the%20Age%20of%20AI">more here</a>.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/foundations-of-power-management-in-the-age-of-ai/">Foundations of Power Management in the Age of AI</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>This white paper examines the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in analog and mixed-signal (AMS) design, where complexity is rising, schedules are tightening, and the cost of mistakes is higher than ever. Drawing on Cadence’s structured AI maturity roadmap and paired with the Virtuoso AI Studio platform, the paper makes the case: AI is no longer a futureworld for analog designers, it has become a present-day engineering tool. From ML-powered engines to conversational design assistance to autonomous, multi-agent workflows, the paper charts a path from where the industry stands today to where it is headed. It also shows how AI can reduce non-differentiating work, accelerate simulation and migration tasks, and serve as a force multiplier for engineers at every experience level, all within a secure, enterprise-ready environment.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>In the AI era, the biggest costs in an SoC project often come from execution, driven by hidden costs that build up when IP is sourced piece by piece from multiple vendors. At advanced nodes, re-spins, integration delays and missed tape-out dates can put millions of dollars at risk. This eBook explains how a single, integrated Foundation IP platform reduces that risk and helps lower TCO. The solution includes silicon-proven logic libraries, embedded memories, IOs and NVM, and it&#8217;s backed by IP + EDA co-optimization and one support team. Using modeled examples from HPC and Edge AI SoCs, it shows how predictable execution can lead to significant savings, from avoided re-spins and schedule slips to measurable power, performance and area (PPA) gains.</p>
<p>You&#8217;ll learn:</p>
<ul>
<li>Why execution risk now drives SoC cost at advanced nodes</li>
<li>The hidden costs of sourcing Foundation IP from multiple vendors</li>
<li>How an integrated IP platform helps lower TCO through faster tape-out, first-pass silicon success and confident node-to-node scaling</li>
<li>How avoiding a single re-spin or schedule slip can save millions on an advanced-node SoC</li>
<li>How PPA gains can translate into measurable savings across HPC and Edge AI designs</li>
</ul>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Agentic solutions for RF design.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/planning-your-ai-design-journey-in-rf-eda/">Planning Your AI Design Journey In RF EDA</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping electronic design automation, creating new opportunities for RF and microwave engineering teams to improve productivity, preserve expertise, and accelerate innovation. As designs become increasingly complex and experienced engineers become harder to replace, organizations must find practical ways to integrate AI into existing workflows without disrupting proven design processes.</p>
<p>This white paper presents a strategic framework for AI adoption built around three complementary themes: Capture, Orchestrate, and Accelerate. Rather than prescribing a single transformation path, the framework enables organizations to pursue one or all three capabilities in parallel using the engineering tools they already rely on, including Advanced Design System (ADS), RFPro, RF Circuit Simulation Pro (Nexus), and Python. Capture focuses on making engineering knowledge reusable by transforming institutional expertise into accessible, repeatable workflows. Orchestrate introduces intelligent agents that automate routine engineering tasks and enable scalable design processes. Accelerate expands design exploration through machine learning, surrogate models, and measurement-correlated simulation to evaluate more design alternatives in less time.</p>

		<title>How Much Can Semiconductor Models Hide?</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/how-much-can-semiconductor-models-hide/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/how-much-can-semiconductor-models-hide/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Gregory Haley]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 07:01:04 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Top Stories]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[advanced packaging]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Amkor]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[ANSYS]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[ASE]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Brewer Science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[chiplets]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[digital twins]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[EDA]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[heterogeneous integration]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[modeling]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[OSATs]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[PDF Solutions]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[reduced-order models]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Silvaco]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[simulation]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[substrates]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Synopsys]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[thermal]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24283339</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Advanced packaging requires models to cross company boundaries without exposing proprietary processes, but hiding too much can make the prediction break down.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/how-much-can-semiconductor-models-hide/">How Much Can Semiconductor Models Hide?</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Advanced packaging pushes process behavior across company lines, so what one supplier hides now shapes another company&#8217;s prediction.</li>
<li>Encryption and abstraction protect the recipe cleanly, but neither tells the receiving engineer where the model stops being valid.</li>
<li>A model can be accurate and still be wrong for the question asked, making its envelope as much a deliverable as the model.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>The goal seems simple — share the model without sharing the process. A materials supplier shouldn’t have to reveal a proprietary formulation just so a customer can predict how it will behave in a package, and a foundry shouldn’t have to hand over its recipe to provide a useful model of a chiplet. But advanced packaging is making that separation much harder to maintain.</p>
<p>For years, engineers moved much of what they needed between companies through datasheets, design rules, and qualification specs, while the manufacturing knowledge stayed with the supplier. That arrangement held as long as the pieces behaved independently, but what one company keeps inside its process now shapes how another company’s part of the package performs once everything is assembled. The process may still belong to the supplier, but its consequences no longer end at the factory gate.</p>
<p>“There’s been some initial work on this challenge, but how do you insert a membrane between the companies so they can share a certain amount of data, but not all,” said Greg Prewitt, director of product management for Exensio Test Operations at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/pdf-solutions/">PDF Solutions</a>. “Do you obfuscate it? Do you normalize it? How much do you share so both teams can solve a problem without seeing any of the IP that’s proprietary to one company or another?”</p>
<p>The difficulty is deciding what that membrane should let through. Hide too little and the supplier gives away process knowledge it spent years developing. Hide too much and the model may lose the behavior, variation, or limits that the engineer on the other side needs to make a useful prediction. That leaves a harder question — how much can disappear inside it before it starts hiding something the prediction actually needs?</p>
<p>Materials show the problem in its simplest form. Engineers may need to know how a material changes with temperature, whether a substrate will warp enough to affect assembly, or how process variation propagates into electrical performance without needing the proprietary details that produced those behaviors. A customer doesn’t need a material company’s formulation to model how one of its materials will behave, but a few static numbers on a datasheet may not be enough either.</p>
<p>“Although proprietary formulations cannot be shared, material characterization across the range of conditions relevant to the intended application can provide a more comprehensive representation of material behavior, allowing models to better reflect real-world conditions and improve prediction accuracy,” said Hanlin Chen, senior research associate and team lead at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/brewer-science/">Brewer Science</a>. “A digital twin that uses single fixed values for material inputs will always underrepresent real-world risk.”</p>
<p><strong>The data handoff challenge<br />
</strong>The need for more detailed models is growing because an advanced package brings together pieces whose engineering histories accumulated in different places. They may pass through several companies before the finished package reaches the system, but by then no single company necessarily has the whole history.</p>
<p>“Advanced packaging is enabled by a highly collaborative supply chain,” said Joon Ahn, vice president of global factory IT and automation at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/amkor-technology/">Amkor</a>. “Dies, substrates, materials, and design information are contributed by multiple partners. Each participant owns unique expertise and data associated with their portion of the value chain.”</p>
<p>That distributed ownership becomes a problem once the design flow needs manufacturing information before everything has been built. The process can remain inside one company, but enough of its behavior has to become usable somewhere else.</p>
<p>What reaches the next engineer is usually enough to describe the part as designed, but not necessarily enough to explain how it will behave after assembly. Nominal dimensions and basic electrical or material properties are relatively easy to pass along. Production variation and the history behind those numbers are much less likely to make the trip.</p>
<p>“I don’t think we need complete data transparency to create a connected digital thread,” said CP Hung, vice president of corporate R&amp;D at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/ase/">ASE</a>. “What we really need is a trusted way to share enough information for the next engineering decision to be made.”</p>
<p>That doesn’t mean every upstream detail belongs in the model. Some can disappear without changing the prediction, while others matter only when something elsewhere in the package exposes their effect. For example, a chiplet’s thermal response may be enough for one analysis, but process variation can change that response in a way the downstream model can’t see.</p>
<p>The question therefore isn’t simply how much information can be shared. It&#8217;s which information still matters after the process itself has been hidden. A model that preserves the right behavior can protect the recipe underneath it. Hide the wrong thing, however, and the uncertainty disappears from the model even though it never disappeared from the package.</p>
<p><strong>How much physics can a model hide?<br />
</strong>Reduced-order and surrogate models solve a similar computational problem in different ways. A reduced-order model simplifies a higher-fidelity physical representation, while a surrogate approximates behavior across a sampled design or process space. Both make analysis practical when running the underlying model every time would take too long, but they don’t become more trustworthy because they run faster.</p>
<p>“The surrogate model can be trusted if the simulated data used to create the surrogate model is accurate,” said Eric Guichard, senior vice president and general manager of AI Manufacturing at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/silvaco-inc/">Silvaco</a>. “For the simulation data to be accurate and predictive, the physical models used to generate them must be calibrated. The calibration can only be done against experimental data. Those experimental data are usually available and not proprietary. Physical model calibration is only one part of the equation. The second part is the knowledge of the detailed process recipes.”</p>
<p>The problem splits into two very different kinds of information. Experimental measurements can provide the evidence needed to calibrate a model without revealing much about the process itself, but building a predictive representation may still require details the company would never hand directly to a customer.</p>
<p>What makes that workable is an asymmetry between building the model and using it. The organization creating the model may need to know enough about the process to establish why it behaves the way it does. The engineer consuming the model may only need access to that behavior. A substrate model, for example, might expose thickness, material response, and the effects of process variation without revealing how the supplier achieves those characteristics in manufacturing.</p>
<p>“If only some key knobs are exposed to the user of the surrogate model, we can reasonably believe that the proprietary process details are preserved,” Guichard said.</p>
<p>The recipe doesn’t disappear. It moves behind the model boundary. But that only relocates the disclosure problem rather than solving it, because the model builder still needs what the supplier is trying to protect.</p>
<p>“Availability of detailed process recipes is actually the challenge,” Guichard added.</p>
<p><strong>Encryption protects proprietary data<br />
</strong>Encryption creates a way to separate useful behavior from proprietary implementation. Synopsys&#8217; HFSS (High Frequency Structure Simulator) supports encrypted electromagnetic models that a component supplier can share for use in a customer’s simulation without exposing the underlying geometry and material information.</p>
<p>“These encrypted models solve a significant but non-technical hurdle — how to share simulation models of an electronic part with your customers without revealing your trade secrets,” said Lang Lin, product management director at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>.</p>
<p>Encryption handles the disclosure problem neatly. The engineer receiving the model can use it without gaining access to what’s sealed inside. What encryption can’t tell that engineer is whether the model is still valid for the problem being asked.</p>
<p>“That has always been one of the key concerns about simulation, in general,&#8221; Lin said. &#8220;How well does it actually match reality?”</p>
<p>A model can be secure and still be wrong for the conditions in which it’s being used. If it was built around one package or process window, the result may remain numerically precise long after the design has moved beyond those conditions. Encryption can make that harder to catch because the user can’t look inside and see where the original assumptions stop holding. The IP can stay perfectly protected while the engineering decision doesn’t.</p>
<p>Model sharing therefore needs something outside the encrypted model itself. The recipient may not need to know how the model works internally, but they still need to know the conditions under which it can be trusted.</p>
<p><strong>When the model stops working<br />
</strong>Materials make that problem easier to see. A datasheet can be perfectly accurate and still describe only one moment in a material’s life. Once that material is cured, assembled, and put into service, the properties used to build the model may start to move.</p>
<p>“A datasheet gives you a snapshot, CTE, modulus, adhesion, viscosity, measured under one set of conditions at one point in time,” said Brewer’s Chen. “Mechanical and thermal properties shift with degree of curing. Crosslink density may continue to evolve after processing, and adhesion strength is highly dependent on the specific bonding interface. CTE also varies, particularly in the temperature region near the polymer’s Tg (glass transition temperature). Treating any of these as a single static number causes a lot of simulation-to-silicon gaps.”</p>
<p>The supplier doesn’t have to reveal the formulation to account for that behavior. What has to survive the handoff is enough information to show how the material changes under the conditions the package is likely to see. A nominal value may be enough at one point in the design space but misleading somewhere else.</p>
<p>Surrogate models make the same validity problem particularly visible. They can be highly accurate inside the region represented by their training data and still return a plausible-looking answer after the user has wandered outside it. The model hasn’t necessarily failed at that point. It’s being asked a question its underlying data was never meant to answer.</p>
<p>“The fundamental principle is that surrogate models are reliable when interpolating within the region represented by their training data and less reliable when extrapolating beyond it,” Guichard said.</p>
<p>The difficulty is that nothing in the output necessarily flags the crossing. A number returned from outside the training region can look exactly like a number returned from inside it.</p>
<p>A useful black box therefore needs a visible envelope around it. The recipe can remain hidden, but the conditions that establish where the model applies can’t. The engineer using it needs to know when the question has moved outside the territory the model actually knows. The model builder has to make that territory visible, and the user still has to respect it.</p>
<p><strong>The interfaces add complexity<br />
</strong>The problem gets harder at the interfaces because the IP line often falls in the same place where two independently built models have to begin describing the same physical behavior.</p>
<p>A material, substrate, or die model may be perfectly valid for the conditions its supplier intended. The trouble starts when those models are joined and the assumptions underneath them don’t line up. One may treat a temperature, geometry, or other condition as fixed while another allows it to move.</p>
<p>“The challenge is that the data often comes in different formats, at different levels of detail, and with different assumptions behind it,” said ASE’s Hung. “A material property, for example, only really means something if we know how it changes with temperature, moisture, time, and process history. A component model may also work perfectly well on its own but not tell us enough about what happens once it’s integrated into the package.”</p>
<p>Those assumptions become harder to separate once the package is assembled. Heat generated in the die moves through the structures around it, while the resulting temperature changes material behavior and mechanical stress elsewhere in the assembly. The models may have been created separately, but the package doesn’t operate that way.</p>
<p>“The real challenge isn’t simply moving data from one company to another,” Hung said. “It’s making sure the physical meaning of that data doesn’t get lost along the way.”</p>
<p>Thermal analysis shows how quickly the information problem follows. Substrate and interposer data may exist upstream, but the downstream design flow needs it in a form that can be combined with the rest of the package.</p>
<p>“When you’re talking about thermal, it’s not just the dies,” said Amlendu Shekhar Choubey, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “This is an integrated problem. You need the whole stack.”</p>
<p>But having all the pieces still doesn’t guarantee they fit. One supplier may characterize behavior under one set of conditions while the model on the other side of the interface assumes another. Even the same nominal parameter can mean something different if it was measured at another temperature, derived from a different process state, or intended for a different range of operation.</p>
<p>The harder problem isn’t getting more data across the interface. The handoff has to preserve enough of the assumptions behind the data for the next model to know how to use it, or every model can be right on its own while the package they describe together is wrong.</p>
<p><strong>What models need to carry<br />
</strong>The model itself is becoming a kind of engineering contract between companies. One side doesn’t promise to expose how a process works. It promises to describe enough of what that process does for another engineer to use the result within an agreed set of conditions. The formulation, recipe, or implementation can stay hidden as long as the model exposes the behavior the next engineer actually needs. The receiving engineer still needs to know what kind of promise is being made.</p>
<p>“Uncertainty and model validity need to move with the model,” said Kenneth Larsen, senior director of 3D-IC product management at Synopsys. “It is not enough to exchange geometry, material properties, or simulation results. Each model also needs to carry the context that determines whether it can be trusted — where the data came from, how it was measured or calibrated, what assumptions were used, what range it is valid over, and what decisions it is intended to support.”</p>
<p>That context matters most when the model is abstracted or encrypted. A model useful for architecture exploration may not be trustworthy for final closure, and a surrogate built inside one process window doesn’t automatically stay predictive after the package changes. The output alone gives the engineer no indication that the original promise no longer applies.</p>
<p>The practical answer isn’t to demand that everything become visible. It’s to make the model’s useful behavior and its limits visible enough that the company receiving it can decide whether it applies.</p>
<p>Supplier boundaries won&#8217;t disappear, and neither will the competitive value of the processes behind them. In many cases those proprietary details are exactly why a customer selected the supplier in the first place. What’s changing is how much engineering information can stop at the boundary with them. A traditional black box could hide both the process and most of its behavior because the customer mainly needed a specification. A model shared into a tightly coupled package has to conceal the recipe while leaving enough of its consequences visible for someone else to make a defensible decision.</p>
<p><strong>Conclusion<br />
</strong>For years, the black box was a workable bargain. A supplier could protect how something was made, the customer could design around a specification, and enough margin usually existed between the two to absorb what neither side could see. Advanced packaging is narrowing that margin because the behavior of one piece increasingly depends on what happened to another before the two ever met.</p>
<p>That doesn’t make proprietary process knowledge less valuable. If anything, the process may become more valuable as packages demand materials, assembly methods, and manufacturing windows tuned to a particular architecture. But the model now has to carry something the old specification often didn’t — enough evidence about what that hidden process does, where that behavior changes, and when the representation should no longer be trusted.</p>
<p>The companies that solve this best probably won’t be the ones that share the most. They’ll be the ones that can turn proprietary process knowledge into models other engineers can use without being able to reconstruct what’s underneath. The recipe can stay private, but the consequences cannot.</p>
<p><strong>Related Articles<br />
</strong><a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-is-rewriting-the-ip-playbook/">AI Is Rewriting The IP Playbook<br />
</a>As the semiconductor ecosystem pivots to AI, it is transforming how IP is created, verified, managed, and sold.</p>
<p><a href="https://semiengineering.com/how-long-does-a-measurement-remain-valid/">How Long Does A Measurement Remain Valid?<br />
</a>Measurements can be misleading after the chip, the test path, or the assumptions behind the result change.</p>
<p><a href="https://semiengineering.com/an-ai-model-fit-for-purpose/">An AI Model Fit For Purpose<br />
</a>Using models outside the context in which they were created for can result in misleading information.</p>

		<title>The imec Report: Scaling Optical Interconnects For The AI Era</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/the-imec-report-scaling-optical-interconnects-for-the-ai-era/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/the-imec-report-scaling-optical-interconnects-for-the-ai-era/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Imene Jadli]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 27 Oct 2026 07:01:34 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Perspectives & Analysis]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[The Imec Report]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[3D integrated optics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[co-packaged optics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[CPO]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[imec]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[interconnects]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[Micro-Transfer Printing]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[OIO3D]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Unprecedented demand for bandwidth calls for bringing optics closer to silicon through a fundamental rethinking of the optical interconnect roadmap.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/the-imec-report-scaling-optical-interconnects-for-the-ai-era/">The imec Report: Scaling Optical Interconnects For The AI Era</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The explosive growth of cloud computing and AI – from generative, and reasoning, to (ultimately) agentic systems – is creating unprecedented demand for bandwidth, as the amount of data that must be moved both within and between data centers continues to surge. In turn, this exposes growing limitations in the underlying interconnects that not only span the data center fabric and rack level but also extend deep inside servers – down to where they link XPUs, memory, and other system components at the package and die level.</p>
<p><strong>Copper-based (electrical) interconnects</strong> have long been the industry’s workhorse thanks to their low cost, simplicity, and reliability. Yet today, they are increasingly hitting fundamental limits: while highly energy-efficient electrical links can be realized, they are typically confined to very short reaches (on the order of millimeters). At longer distances and higher lane rates, power consumption rises sharply, thermal constraints intensify, and signal integrity degrades. In other words, electrical I/O is rapidly becoming a key barrier to scaling next-generation AI and machine learning systems.</p>
<p><strong>Optical interconnects</strong> have emerged as a critical path forward. By transmitting data using light rather than electrical signals, they are far less sensitive to distance, enabling much better energy efficiency while mitigating many of the crosstalk and thermal challenges inherent to copper links. However, even optical technologies are now being pushed to new extremes – as the need emerges for (multi) terabit-per-second interfaces, ultra-high energy efficiency, and extremely low (sub-microsecond) latency.</p>
<p>Meeting these requirements will take more than incremental innovation. It calls for a fundamental rethinking of the optical interconnect roadmap; one that progressively brings optics closer to the silicon – from the front panel, into the package, and ultimately firmly integrated into the wafer stack.</p>
<h2>Pluggable optics (PO): The longstanding – and still very much alive – workhorse</h2>
<p>For more than two decades, <strong>pluggable optical transceivers</strong> have been the backbone of high-speed telecom and datacom networks – powering everything from enterprise workloads and video streaming to today’s hyperscale cloud infrastructure. Inserted into standardized ports on switches, routers, and servers, pluggables convert electrical signals from the host into optical signals for transmission over fiber – and back again on the receive side.</p>
<p>They deliver:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Modularity and flexibility</strong> – optics can be upgraded independently of the (electrical) host.</li>
<li><strong>Serviceability</strong> – pluggables are hot-swappable, meaning they can be replaced without system downtime.</li>
<li><strong>Multi-vendor interoperability</strong> – achieved via IEEE 802.3 standards, and through widely-adopted multi-source agreement (MSA) form factors such as QSFP, QSFP-DD, and OSFP.</li>
<li><strong>Thermal stability</strong> – the optical engine sits in a front-panel cage, physically separated from the power‑dense ASIC; this helps protect lasers, modulators, and photodetectors from excessive heat (improving reliability).</li>
</ul>
<p>Across successive generations, pluggable optical transceivers have scaled from 100/200G to 400G and 800G by pushing baud rates (the number of symbols transmitted per second on a single optical lane), adopting higher-order modulation (such as PAM-4), and increasing the number of parallel lanes.</p>
<p>And despite their maturity, pluggable optics continue to evolve. First-generation <strong>1.6T pluggable transceivers</strong>, for instance – relying on 200Gbps per-lane data rates, combined in an eight-lane parallel architecture – are approaching sampling and early deployment, targeting direct-reach (DR) intra-data center links as well as forward-reach (FR) connections over single-mode fiber.</p>
<p>The key enabler is <strong>silicon photonics (SiPho)</strong>, which underpins this scaling through a combination of (silicon-based) optical and electronic building blocks, including Mach–Zehnder modulators that play a central role in enabling cost-effective 200Gbps per-lane operation while keeping power consumption in check.</p>
<p>Looking further ahead, toward the end of the decade, the industry is eyeing the <strong>3.2T pluggable optics </strong>milestone. Yet, achieving these performance levels will require continued advances in high-speed electronics, packaging, and thermal management – as well as a substantial expansion of the silicon photonics (SiPho) toolbox. On the transmit side, for instance, optical modulators will need to support bandwidths beyond 100GHz while maintaining low insertion loss and high modulation efficiency – requirements that are becoming increasingly difficult to meet with conventional silicon devices alone.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283328" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig1.webp?resize=906%2C445&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="906" height="445" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig1.webp?w=906&amp;ssl=1 906w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C147&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C377&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C295&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 906px) 100vw, 906px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Pluggable optics have delivered an order-of-magnitude leap in performance in the past few years – both in bandwidth density and power efficiency. Source: imec.</strong></p>
<p>Addressing these limitations is driving interest in the <strong>heterogeneous integration of higher-performance electro-optic materials</strong> such as lithium niobate (LiNbO₃) and lithium tantalate (LiTaO₃). Techniques such as <strong>micro-transfer printing</strong> offer a promising path to integrate these materials onto silicon photonics platforms. Early results are encouraging, but further research is ongoing to scale these approaches to high-volume manufacturing – so that future 3.2T modules can be built with the same practicality, reliability, and cost discipline that made pluggable optics the industry’s workhorse in the first place.</p>
<p>In parallel, alternative scaling approaches are also being explored. Concepts such as <strong>extreme pluggable optics (XPO)</strong> target capacities up to 12.8T by further increasing bandwidth density, albeit at the expense of significantly higher system complexity and the need for liquid cooling, which – at least for now – impacts both cost and practical deployment.</p>
<h3>A double world-first: Integrating LiNbO₃ and LiTaO₃ on SiPho via micro-transfer printing</h3>
<p>As optical interconnects (need to) push beyond today’s 200Gbps-per-lane standard, GeSi-based devices increasingly struggle to deliver the required combination of bandwidth and energy efficiency. While GeSi modulators have demonstrated scaling to 400Gbps per lane in the C-band, such performance has not yet been achieved in the O-band. To unlock the next performance leap in pluggable optical interconnects, researchers are therefore investigating the heterogeneous integration of advanced electro-optic materials – such as lithium niobate (LiNbO₃) and lithium tantalate (LiTaO₃) – onto silicon photonics, paving the way for a new class of high-speed modulators and photodetectors.</p>
<p>A promising enabler is <strong>micro-transfer printing</strong>, which enables the precise placement of thin-film materials onto SiPho wafers without the material waste, post-bonding complexity, and cost typically associated with conventional wafer bonding. Two world-first results highlight its potential:</p>
<p>First, researchers from imec and Ghent University showcased an O-band 320Gbps unamplified optical link over 2km of single-mode fiber. This was achieved using a high-bandwidth 100GHz germanium photodiode in combination with transfer-printed thin-film lithium niobate Mach-Zehnder modulators (MZMs), integrated onto a SiPho platform and co-packaged with custom-designed traveling-wave drivers and TIAs. This work marked the first seamless integration of LiNbO₃ modulators onto a silicon photonics platform using micro-transfer printing.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283329" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=1544%2C1030&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1544" height="1030" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?w=1544&amp;ssl=1 1544w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C200&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=1024%2C683&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=768%2C512&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=1536%2C1025&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=600%2C400&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: The first seamless integration of LiNbO₃ modulators onto a silicon photonics platform using micro-transfer printing. Source: imec.</strong></p>
<p>The team also achieved the first-ever heterogeneous integration of a LiTaO₃ modulator on a silicon photonic integrated circuit. Using the same micro-transfer printing technique previously applied to lithium niobate, the researchers achieved full compatibility with the entire wafer stack, enabling co-integration with other photonic building blocks such as heaters, filters, and germanium photodetectors without compromising their performance.</p>
<p>While these modulators are still relatively large, they offer a viable path for further scaling pluggable transceivers, where footprint constraints are less stringent. At the same time, alternative device concepts are being explored to meet the tighter size and integration requirements of future <strong>co-packaged optics</strong>. These include compact, ultra-high-speed GeSi-based modulators operating in the C-band, as well as emerging approaches based on the integration of III-V materials into silicon photonics platforms.</p>
<p>Further work is required to scale these heterogeneous integration approaches to high-volume manufacturing. Nevertheless, the results highlight a promising route toward integrating &gt;100GHz electro-optic devices on SiPho – a capability widely seen as essential for future 3.2T pluggable modules and next-generation optical interconnects supporting AI-driven infrastructure.</p>
<h2>Fast-and-narrow co-packaged optics (CPO): A key pillar of the optical interconnect roadmap</h2>
<p>Pluggable optics, however, are not the answer to every challenge. The rapid rise of (generative) AI workloads is pushing optical (inter)connectivity ever deeper into compute servers and accelerator clusters – all the way down to the chip-to-chip level.</p>
<p>At this scale, a new set of constraints emerges. Pluggable optical transceivers rely on very high baud rates, in combination with sophisticated digital signal processing (DSP) to compensate for signal degradation. While this works well at the rack or data center level, the power consumption and latency associated with heavy DSP become increasingly problematic for short-reach, <strong>chip-to-chip optical interconnects </strong>in AI and machine learning systems. Instead, they require intrinsically clean optical channels with extremely low bit-error rates, allowing each lane to operate without excessive equalization or DSP overhead.</p>
<p>This shift is precisely what drives the adoption of <strong>fast-and-narrow co-packaged optics (CPO)</strong>. In a CPO system, the optical components are placed in close physical proximity to the (switching) silicon or compute die, shrinking the electrical path from several centimeters (as in pluggables) to just a few millimeters – or even less. By moving the electro-optic conversion point directly adjacent to the ASIC (within the same package), CPO greatly improves signal integrity, minimizes electrical losses, and reduces latency – without relying on power-hungry DSP. This makes CPO a compelling architecture for scaling next-generation AI and high-performance compute systems.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283330" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?resize=1202%2C598&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1202" height="598" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?w=1202&amp;ssl=1 1202w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?resize=300%2C149&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?resize=1024%2C509&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?resize=768%2C382&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?resize=600%2C299&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 3: Co-packaged optics shorten the electrical path between the optical engine and the host IC, enabling higher bandwidth density and eliminating the need for digital signal processing, thereby improving power efficiency. Source: imec.</strong></p>
<p>But as early CPO deployments begin to emerge, integration complexity remains one of the defining challenges of the technology. Unlike pluggable optics – where the optical module is (largely) self-contained – CPO requires <strong>tight co-design and co-optimization</strong>, including photonic integrated circuits (PICs), electronic ICs (EICs), switch ASICs, fiber‑coupling strategies, thermal management, and advanced packaging. Addressing this multidisciplinary challenge is a central objective of imec’s Optical Interconnect Program.</p>
<p>In the CPO domain (also referred to as OIO2.5D), imec’s key research targets include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Scaling optical engine capacity from 1.6T and 3.2T, toward 6.4T and ultimately 12.8T.</li>
<li>Enabling fast-and-narrow 400Gbps lane rates, and achieving bandwidth densities approaching 1Tbps per millimeter.</li>
<li>Facilitating energy efficiencies up to 5pJ/bit, trending toward 3pJ/bit in future technology generations.</li>
<li>Integrating the full optical stack – modulators, photo detectors, couplers, fiber attach, and thermal solutions – within a manufacturable package.</li>
</ul>
<p>Reaching these targets depends heavily on advanced semiconductor packaging technologies that support dense integration of photonic and electronic components – think of 2.5D interposer architectures, through-silicon vias (TSVs), fan-out wafer-level packaging (FO-WLP), and (increasingly) 3D integration enabled by hybrid bonding – as well as the use of advanced (III-V) materials.</p>
<p>And then there’s the light source. While the long-term goal is to integrate lasers directly on the photonic chip, early CPO systems will still rely on <strong>externally mounted laser sources</strong>. This approach simplifies thermal management and mitigates long-standing reliability concerns of operating lasers near hot ASICs. The trade-offs: higher output power to compensate for optical losses, greater packaging complexity, and the need for additional fibers and connectors to route light into the package.</p>
<h3>Realizing the first net-400Gbps per-lane transmission with a silicon-based EAM</h3>
<p>In October 2025, imec announced a major advance for next‑generation optical interconnects: a beyond-110GHz C-band GeSi electro-absorption modulator (EAM) delivering a net data rate of 400Gbps per lane.</p>
<p>Leveraging the Franz-Keldysh effect, the device combines compact size, high speed, and low power consumption. And thanks to its GeSi foundation, it integrates seamlessly on 300mm CMOS-compatible SiPho platforms, offering a clear route to high-volume manufacturability.</p>
<p>This breakthrough reflects more than a decade of coordinated progress at both the device and system levels. On the device side, imec optimized footprint, doping schemes, and epitaxial growth processes. At the system level, a robust PAM-4 IM/DD transmission setup validated sustained net-400Gbps per-lane operation, demonstrating the practical readiness of GeSi EAM technology for future high-lane-rate optical engines.</p>
<h2>3D integrated optics (OIO3D): The next frontier</h2>
<p>As AI and machine learning systems scale to thousands of tightly interconnected accelerators, each linked to high-bandwidth memory stacks and peer processors over distances of only a few millimeters, the demands placed on optical interconnects become even more extreme. Over the next decade, they are expected to support bandwidth densities approaching (and surpassing) 10Tbps/mm, energy efficiencies well below 1pJ/bit, and ultra-low latencies (&lt;100ns). These targets extend beyond what even advanced CPO architectures can achieve.</p>
<p>To meet these requirements, optics must move beyond the package and into the wafer stack itself. This is the foundation of <strong>3D integrated optics</strong>. By collapsing the electrical path to micrometer-scale distances, OIO3D enables ultra-short, high-bandwidth, and energy-efficient optical links that make dense chip-to-chip optical fabrics feasible.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283331" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?resize=1202%2C606&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1202" height="606" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?w=1202&amp;ssl=1 1202w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?resize=300%2C151&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?resize=1024%2C516&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?resize=768%2C387&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?resize=600%2C302&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 4: By collapsing the electrical path to micrometer-scale distances, OIO3D enables ultra-short, high-bandwidth, and energy-efficient optical links that make dense chip-to-chip optical fabrics feasible. Source: imec.</strong></p>
<p>Realizing 3D integrated optics requires overcoming several major technology challenges. These include scalable laser integration, the development of high-efficiency, high-bandwidth electro-optic components (e.g., based on GeSi, lithium niobate, lithium tantalate, indium phosphide, or barium titanate), and robust thermal management in densely stacked environments. Equally crucial are ultra-precise bonding and alignment techniques at wafer scale.</p>
<h3>OIO2.5D vs OIO3D</h3>
<p>An evolutionary step beyond CPO, <strong>OIO2.5D</strong> combines high‑density photonic integration with manageable packaging complexity by placing photonic and electronic dies side‑by‑side on a shared silicon interposer. Photonic layers are integrated using die‑to‑wafer Cu‑based hybrid bonding, a technique that enables ultrashort, low‑parasitic electrical paths.</p>
<p>This architecture initially targets optical engines in the 8-32Tbps range. It leverages 32-64 Gbps per‑lane rates, optimized for low‑power, DSP‑free operation to minimize latency and heat. Wavelength‑division multiplexing (8-32 wavelengths per fiber) further boosts aggregate bandwidth without increasing fiber count. The technology roadmap aims for bandwidth densities of 2Tbps per millimeter and energy efficiencies near 2 pJ/bit.</p>
<p><strong>OIO3D</strong> represents the most advanced and ambitious vision for optical interconnects. Here, photonic layers are stacked directly above or below the compute silicon, creating a true chip‑scale optical fabric that collapses electrical paths to micrometer‑scale distances.</p>
<p>This approach relies on both die‑to‑wafer and wafer‑to‑wafer hybrid bonding, enabling extremely fine‑pitch vertical interconnects. With this level of vertical integration, OIO3D aims to extend bandwidth capabilities to tens of terabits per second (and beyond), while targeting energy efficiencies around 2 pJ/bit – with a longer‑term trajectory toward sub‑pJ/bit operation.</p>
<p>A key research vector is on‑wafer laser integration, using heterogeneous III‑V approaches such as quantum‑dot GaAs‑on‑Si. This is actively being explored within the EU Chips Act pilot lines for future large‑scale photonic systems.</p>
<h3>Integration of barium titanate on a 300mm SiPho platform</h3>
<p>In January 2026, Veeco Instruments Inc. and imec announced a 300mm high-volume-manufacturing-compatible process for integrating barium titanate (BaTiO<sub>3</sub>, BTO) on silicon photonics.</p>
<p>With exceptional electro-optic properties, BTO enables high-speed, low-power modulators for applications ranging from optical transceivers to quantum photonics, LiDAR, and AR/VR. Historically, however, bringing BTO to silicon at scale has been difficult due to cost, uniformity, and manufacturability constraints.</p>
<p>Leveraging a collaboration with imec, Veeco recently delivered its first molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) cluster system tailored for 300mm wafers. The platform supports the growth of single-crystalline BTO thin films on silicon – using solid and hybrid MBE – improving repeatability, material quality, and cost of ownership compared with conventional MBE solutions.</p>
<h2>A look at timelines</h2>
<p>Looking across the evolution of optical interconnects, it is clear the different approaches are progressing along different timelines.</p>
<p><strong>Pluggable optics</strong>, already deployed at global scale, are entering a phase dominated by incremental technical optimizations rather than fundamental breakthroughs. Their roadmap continues – toward 1.6T and 3.2T modules – and pluggables will remain competitive for many use cases while new architectures ramp up.</p>
<p><strong>Co-packaged optics</strong> are also approaching a stage of (relative) maturity. Key building blocks are transitioning into pilot-line support, supply-chain preparation, and wafer-level services – even as the industry continues to pursue higher bandwidth, faster lane rates, and better energy efficiency. The start of broad, large-scale CPO deployments is expected from 2027/2028 onward.</p>
<p><strong>3D integrated optics</strong> remain in an earlier R&amp;D stage. Current efforts focus on pathfinding and building the device/integration toolbox. First proof-of-concept demonstrators are anticipated within three to five years, with wider commercialization expected on a five- to ten-year horizon.</p>
<h3>Bringing next-generation optical interconnects to market</h3>
<p>Through its <a href="https://www.imec-int.com/en/expertise/cmos-advanced/connect/optical-interconnects">optical interconnects research program</a>, imec develops the key building blocks for future optical transceivers, anticipating market needs years before commercial deployment.</p>
<p>Imec’s strength lies in being a true one-stop R&amp;D environment, bringing together expertise in silicon photonics, advanced CMOS, 3D integration, materials research, and system-level modeling. This breadth allows researchers to explore novel concepts far more rapidly than is possible in high-volume manufacturing settings, enabling short development cycles, and the freedom to pursue unconventional (integration) approaches. The program is further strengthened by imec’s <a href="https://www.imec-int.com/en/expertise/cmos-advanced-and-beyond/xtco">cross-technology optimization (XTCO)</a> strategy, which drives scaling across technology domains.</p>
<p>A critical accelerator is the close collaboration between imec’s optical interconnect research teams and <a href="https://www.imeciclink.com/en">IC-Link</a>, imec’s semiconductor manufacturing pillar. While imec’s early‑stage research focuses on pathfinding and prototyping, IC‑Link helps bring technologies toward higher technology‑readiness levels by refining process flows, improving manufacturability, establishing test strategies, and engaging the broader supply chain. Through IC-Link, industrial partners can also access and evaluate these technologies via imec&#8217;s 200mm and 300mm iSiPP silicon photonics platforms, providing a pathway from early-stage innovation to industrial deployment.</p>
<p>Beyond IC-Link, imec maintains close engagement with industrial partners through a variety of collaboration models. These span guided projects (in which imec and its partners jointly explore emerging technologies), to targeted bilateral programs (driven by partner-specific requirements), all the way to long-term core partner engagements. In parallel, imec collaborates closely with equipment suppliers, enabling early validation of advanced tools and process capabilities – well before they enter commercial use.</p>
<p>Together, these interactions ensure that imec’s optical interconnect research stays firmly grounded in real‑world system requirements, while accelerating the translation of advanced technologies into market-ready solutions.</p>
<p><em>Peter Ossieur received the M.Sc. degree in electrical engineering from Ghent University, Belgium in 2000, and the PhD degree in electrical engineering from the same university in 2005. From 2005 till 2009 he was a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University, after which he joined Tyndall National Institute, where he became senior staff researcher. His research interests included electronic integrated circuit design and optical transmission systems. In 2017, he joined imec-IDlab, an imec embedded group at Ghent University. Today, he is director for XTCO Fabric and Optical Interconnect at imec, and holds a parttime appointment as professor at Ghent University. Peter Ossieur is a member of the ISSCC wireline subcommittee.</em></p>
